title: June Snow When Frankenstein Was Born? The 1816 Mystery｜Curio Archive
description:
In June 1816, three days of heavy snow buried North American cornfields before thermometers shot up to 101°F just over two weeks later; that same summer, cold rain trapped an 18-year-old British girl inside a lakeside villa in Geneva, where she began writing Frankenstein — was all of it really caused by an Indonesian volcanic eruption the year before?

For anyone who has heard of the "Year Without a Summer" or that "a volcano gave birth to Frankenstein" and wants to check those claims against 1815 eyewitness reports, weather diaries, polar ice cores, and modern climate attribution models.

Illustrations and narration in this episode were produced with AI assistance.

l001.text: Sweating in summer heat, ever wish it'd snow in June?

l004.text: Same month, rain poured in Geneva,

l005.text: and an 18-year-old Brit indoors began Frankenstein.

l006.text: A year prior, a volcano in Indonesia

l007.text: had just blown its summit apart.

l008.text: Yet no record then blamed that volcano;

l009.text: it took nearly 100 years to link the two.

l011.text: Honestly, checking the files shocked me.

l013.text: yet climate models and her preface say otherwise.

l014.text: Today let's unpack this Year Without a Summer, and see what's the volcano's and what's myth?

l016.text: Java and Makassar officials heard booms all afternoon.

l017.text: It sounded like cannon, so troops sailed out;

l018.text: yet not one enemy ship was out there—what was that?

l019.text: Hundreds of kilometers off, who'd guess a peak?

l020.text: Raffles in Java gathered reports to see:

l021.text: at 7 PM April 10, Sumbawa's ruler of Sanggar saw

l022.text: three huge fire columns shoot from Tambora.

l023.text: The April 10–11 climax reached explosivity index 7,

l024.text: the largest eruption in recorded history.

l025.text: Its peak collapsed 6 to 7 km wide and over 1 km deep,

l026.text: worse still—what happened to daytime afar?

l027.text: At 9 AM April 12, far away in Gresik, Java,

l028.text: falling ash turned broad daylight pitch-black.

l030.text: thousands died; famine took tens of thousands.

l033.text: But volcanic ash settles in days,

l037.text: Oppenheimer put it at 60 million tons,

l039.text: In the stratosphere, sulfate aerosols circled Earth,

l040.text: veiling Earth and dimming sunlight for 3 years.

l043.text: Stothers wrote Northern Hemisphere, not global;

l044.text: stranger still, did the South cool?

l045.text: Per Raible, the tropics and North cooled 0.4 to 0.8°C below the prior 30 years,

l047.text: How those aerosols split north to south is unsolved.

l048.text: Under 1 degree? You'd laugh—that's less than nudging the AC!

l050.text: In one region's summer, cold blasts hit crops head-on—

l053.text: Baltimore's Niles' Weekly noted snow hit on June 6.

l054.text: Quebec snowed 3 days; blizzards hit Maine;

l055.text: papers said Cabot, Vermont saw 18 inches—calf-deep snow.

l058.text: Think it stayed icy? Keep short sleeves.

l062.text: Two days later, noon fell to 59°F;

l064.text: Niles' Weekly noted drought hurt most of the US even worse,

l065.text: dry seedlings got hit by more frosts.

l067.text: and likely sped up New England farmers moving away.

l068.text: Oddly, while US farmers waited for rain,

l069.text: across the ocean in Geneva, the sky left the tap running.

l070.text: Young British visitors walked into that rain—what happened there?

l071.text: In Geneva, records from that summer show

l072.text: summer rain jumped 80% and afternoon highs fell 3.8°C.

l073.text: Late May, Mary Godwin and poet Shelley rented a lake house;

l074.text: 8 minutes off lay Byron's Villa Diodati.

l075.text: Mary wrote: endless rain confines us indoors.

l076.text: Rained in on vacation with no phone—what next?

l077.text: Huddled by the villa's wood fire,

l078.text: with German ghost tales in French.

l079.text: Byron proposed: let's each write a ghost story!

l080.text: Byron, Shelley, doctor Polidori, and Mary agreed.

l081.text: Some say her June 16 diary says so—did it?

l082.text: Biographer Marshall noted her June 1816 diary was lost!

l083.text: The real dated record is Polidori's own diary:

l084.text: On June 17 he wrote: all but me have begun ghost stories.

l086.text: Shelley screamed, grabbed a candle, and fled!

l088.text: In her 1831 preface, asked daily for a plot,

l091.text: but the real turn came at night.

l092.text: A late-night parlor talk suddenly sparked her mind—what was it about?

l093.text: Byron and Shelley debated life's nature,

l094.text: and electricity waking a pieced-up body.

l096.text: she saw a pale student kneeling by the giant form he pieced.

l098.text: it hit her: what scared me will terrify readers!

l099.text: Next morning, she had her story.

l100.text: Ever hear she finished the whole novel by Lake Geneva?

l101.text: The first preface says it began there;

l102.text: wed back in England, she finished by May 1817.

l104.text: who knew it'd pioneer modern sci-fi?

l105.text: In July 1816, Byron wrote Darkness: was it about that weather?

l106.text: It opens: I dreamed the bright sun died.

l107.text: Yet 1901 notes cite literary sources, not weather;

l108.text: calling it a weather log is later spin.

l109.text: Writers in the villa just wrote ghost tales,

l110.text: outside, farmers watching wheat rot couldn't laugh.

l111.text: That wet summer wasn't the worst—

l112.text: what bill hit ordinary Europeans next year?

l113.text: With stores gone, famine erupted in 1817!

l114.text: A Zurich famine broadsheet shows grain peaked in June.

l116.text: potatoes tripled in a year, from 6 francs to 18 or 20.

l117.text: Harvests ran dry by spring across Europe;

l120.text: Barker and Cheyne: 1.5 million sick, over 65,000 dead.

l122.text: stranger still, Tambora's eruption was already in European papers!

l124.text: Remember nobody blamed a volcano? Bodenmann checked—zero linked them.

l125.text: Some blamed sunspots or North Atlantic ice,

l128.text: Press and crowds blamed rods for the rain.

l129.text: Copper rods took the fall while the real culprit hid above.

l130.text: Even wilder, in the late 19th century, the Royal Society still missed the truth—how?

l136.text: The first known Tambora cold-summer link

l138.text: Page 161 notes cold summer followed it.

l139.text: Remember that gap? It took a full 98 years.

l143.text: In 1991, Dai's team matched Greenland and Antarctic cores,

l144.text: ancient ice froze each year's dust.

l145.text: The cores nailed Tambora's sulfate layer,

l146.text: and caught a mystery eruption six years before it.

l147.text: Sulfur in the ice—so "volcano made Frankenstein" is airtight?

l148.text: What a neat butterfly effect, right!

l150.text: Ice didn't answer: what caused Europe's cold and rain?

l151.text: In 2019, attribution models cracked that causal chain—what broke?

l152.text: Schurer's team modeled air patterns and volcano apart,

l153.text: and found cold and rain split up!

l154.text: Airflow caused a quarter of the chill;

l155.text: adding Tambora raised cold odds up to 100-fold!

l156.text: Rain flipped: airflow alone could dump that freak rain;

l159.text: What trapped them inside for ghost tales was rain!

l160.text: In Mary's prefaces and Swiss tour:

l161.text: zero volcano mentions, just a rockslide—how did myths grow?

l163.text: a 2023 medical paper copied text and put Tambora in the Philippines!

l164.text: When even countries get botched, myths harden into fact;

l165.text: in the files, truth beats the legend.

l167.text: Northern cooling and cold-summer odds belong to Tambora's sulfur;

l168.text: airflow alone could make the rain behind Frankenstein,

l169.text: cold rain and moonlight birthed it.

l170.text: If you heard "a volcano made Frankenstein," or saw wild weather, tell me!

l171.text: We check primary files and show gaps;

l172.text: subscribe if you love digging to the bottom—case archived.
